body.p: The Office Action dated October 17, 2024, and the references cited therein have been carefully studied and reviewed, and in view of the following representations, reconsideration is respectfully requested.
By this Amendment, claims 15, 18 and 19 have been revised for clarity. The scope of the claims has not been altered.
Claims 1-20 remain pending in the application.
Claim Objections
By this Amendment, claim 18 has been revised to correct the typographical error identified by the Examiner. It is therefore required that the objection to the claims be withdrawn.
By this Amendment, claims 15, 18 and 19 have been revised as suggested by the Examiner. It is therefore requested that the rejection under 35 U.S.C. § 112(b) be withdrawn.

Claims 1-3, 6, 8, 11, 13 and 15-16 were rejected under 35 U.S.C. §103 as being unpatentable over Yamashita (US 2010275918) in view of Humberstone (US 5518179). Claim 4 was rejected under 35 U.S.C. § 103 as being unpatentable over Yamashita in view of Humberstone and Miller (US 10993657). Claim 5 was rejected under 35 U.S.C. § 103 as being unpatentable over Yamashita in view Humberstone and Rogers (US 20180064377) and Rao (US 20180249935). Claim 7 was rejected under 35 U.S.C. §103 as being unpatentable over Yamashita in view of Humberstone and Weitz (US 20170321177) and Prasad (US 20190069818). Claims 9, 14 and 20 were rejected under 35 U.S.C. §103 as
being unpatentable over Yamashita in view of Humberstone and Bandaru (US

20130079605). Claims 10 was rejected under 35 U.S.C. §103 as being unpatentable over Yamashita in view of Humberstone and Bandaru and Heikenfeld (US 20180353748). Claims 12 was rejected under 35 U.S.C. §103 as being unpatentable over Yamashita in view of Humberstone and Heikenfeld.
Applicant traverses these rejections.
For several reasons, a person of ordinary skill in the art (POSITA) would not combine the teachings of Yamashita and Humberstone in the fashion suggested by the Examiner.
Firstly, Humberstone is "non-analogous art". Please see M.P.E.P. §2141.01(I):

"In order for a reference to be proper for use in an obviousness rejection under 35 U.S.C. 103, the reference must be analogous art to the claimed invention. In re Bigio, 381 F.3d 1320, 1325, 72 USPQ2d 1209, 1212 (Fed. Cir.

2004). A reference is analogous art to the claimed invention if: (1) the reference is from the same field of endeavor as the claimed invention (even if it addresses a different problem); or (2) the reference is reasonably pertinent to the problem faced by the inventor (even if it is not in the same field of endeavor as the claimed invention). ... If a reference is not analogous art to the claimed invention, it may not be used in
an obviousness rejection under 35 U.S.C. 103."
Humberstone is not in the same field of endeavor as the claimed
invention. Specifically, as stated in its Abstract and elsewhere, the field of endeavor of

Humberstone is a fluid droplet production apparatus for use in an atomizer spraying device. In clear contrast, the field of endeavor of the present claims is systems for sensing sweat from a human subject. There is no overlap in the respective fields of endeavor of Humberstone and the claimed invention.
Further, Humberstone is not reasonably pertinent to the problem faced by the present inventors.
The problems faced by present inventors are described in the background section of the present application, exemplary passages of which are reproduced below for convenience.

"Efforts have been made to address these issues by bringing wearable sensors into nearly immediate contact with sweat as it emerges from the skin. A very recent example is the wearable patch presented by Gao et al. in "Fully integrated wearable sensor arrays for multiplexed in situ perspiration analysis" ... . However, the focus of this study is on the development and the integration of the sensors themselves which, whilst evidently crucial, does not
address issues relating to sweat sample collection.

The latter is mostly done by placing a several cm2 sized absorbent pad between the skin and the sensor. The assumption is that, providing ample sweat is produced (hence tests are always done on individuals that heavily exercise), the pad will absorb the sweat for analysis, and newly generated sweat will refill the pad and 'rinse away' the old sweat. It is, however, likely that the time- dependent response of the sensor does not directly reflect the actual level of biomarkers over time because of

accumulation effects. The sample collection and presentation to the published sensors may not be well- controlled so that continuous reliable sensing over a long period of time is difficult. Such patches may also not be designed to handle the tiny amounts of sweat that are produced under normal conditions, i.e. in the order of
nanoliters per minute per sweat gland.

Thus, improvements are required to existing devices for continuous or intermittent monitoring. The detection of biomarkers or analytes in the bio fluid of interest tends to require the device to include a sensor unit having a surface on which capture species are immobilized, which capture
species bind the biomarker.
Access to sweat is limited and uneven especially for individuals at rest in a non-thermal neutral state (i.e.,

outside the thermal neutral zone in which the core body temperature remains very stable and there is no reason to induce sweat production for cooling down the body; typically, 25-30 °C for a naked person at rest or 13-22 °C for a clothed individual) who have sweat rates as low as ~0.03- 0.10 nL/min/gland.
There remain problems of biomarker sensing of very small volumes of sweat of the order of nL/min/gland.

The filling time of microfluidic devices is then long and there is a substantial time delay between the sweat excretion to the skin and actual measurement, which can be as much as several hours of delay." (Emphasis added.)
In short, the problems faced by the inventors relate to biomarker sensing of very small volumes of sweat, especially for individuals at rest in a non-thermal state.

On the other hand, Humberstone in its background section describes a number of prior art sprayers, and states that these "methods generally have low efficiency of energy utilisation in the production of the droplet spray or are of relatively high manufacturing cost." Humberstone also aims to "improve the simplicity" of sprayer devices. There is nothing at all in the disclosure of Humberstone that is pertinent to the problems faced by the present inventors.

Indeed, it can only be through hindsight reconstruction based on present inventors' solution that one would (incorrectly) conclude that Humberstone is reasonably pertinent to the problem faced by the inventors. In fact, however, when properly comparing Humberstone to the problems faced by the inventors, the only reasonable conclusion is that Humberstone is not at all pertinent to those problems.
For at least these reasons, Humberstone is not analogous art and therefore cannot be applied in an obviousness rejection against the now-pending claims.
Further, even assuming arguendo that Humberstone is analogous art (which it is not), it would not be obvious to apply the teachings of Humberstone to the system Yamashita.

First, as explained above, Humberstone is directed to spray or aerosol devices where a substantial source of liquid is assumed to be available (e.g., liquid source 2 of FIGS. 1 and 3). Indeed, as shown in FIG. 1 below, the source 2 of liquid is sufficient enough that a capillary feed 3 is utilized to feed the liquid to a perforated membrane 5.

In direct contrast, Yamashita requires the extraction of body fluid from the subject's skin. No source of liquid is readily available. The record is devoid of any suggestion or teaching that the spray device of Humberstone would even be capable of extracting body fluid from the skin of a subject. In this respect, note that Yamashita relies on application of a "body fluid discharge promoting medicine" to induce the discharge of body fluid. Indeed, as shown below, separate subsystems are provided to supply and collect this medicine.

M.P.E.P. §2142: The key to supporting any rejection under 35 U.S.C. 103 is the clear articulation of the reason(s) why the claimed invention would have been obvious. The Supreme Court in KSR Int'l Co. v. Teleflex Inc., 550 U.S.
538, 418, 82 USPQ2d 1385, 1396 (2007) noted that the analysis supporting a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 103 should be made explicit. The Federal Circuit has stated that
"rejections on obviousness cannot be sustained with mere conclusory statements; instead, there must be some articulated reasoning with some rational underpinning
to support the legal conclusion of obviousness." (Emphasis
added.)

Respectfully, the Examiner's rejection lacks the requisite articulated reasoning with some rational underpinning to support the legal conclusion of obviousness. Nothing in Humberstone, which draws liquid through capillary action from a substantial source of liquid, would lead the POSITA to believe the extraction of liquid from human skin is reasonably possible as an alternative application. Further, use of the membrane of Humberstone would clearly impede the application and collection of body fluid discharge promoting medicine of Yamashita, both of which are central to overall design of Yamashita.

For at least these reasons, the now-pending claims are not obvious over the combination of Yamashita and Humberstone. Further, the remaining applied references do not overcome the deficiencies in the teaching Yamashita and Humberstone.
It is therefore requested that the rejections under 35 U.S.C. § 103 be withdrawn.

In view of the foregoing explanations, Applicant respectfully requests that the Examiner reconsider and reexamine the present application and pass the application to issue.
